title: The Breastplate
hook: Patrick's lorica: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ in every eye that sees me
tomorrow: what hangs on the wall of a monk's workshop?

segments.voice: That was a week of the early Church in its own words: an anvil, an old bishop's witness, a Sunday written out, a ladder, a flame, and a laugh in a tomb. Yesterday's line: laughing at demons.
screen: `LAUGHING AT DEMONS.` → `THE EARLY CHURCH, IN ITS OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Keys, phone, jacket. Before the door, everyone has a little routine of things to put on. Soldiers once strapped on a breastplate. An old Irish prayer straps on something else: armor made of words. Tradition puts it in the mouth of Saint Patrick, and a story people tell says he and his companions sang it on a road where enemies lay in wait, and the enemies saw only deer passing by.
screen: `KEYS, PHONE, JACKET.` → `ARMOR MADE OF WORDS.` → `ONLY DEER PASSING BY.`

segments.voice: First, the name. It's often called a lorica, the Latin word for body armor, and Paul uses the same picture when he speaks of the breastplate of justice. Second, the strength. The singer rises each day through the power of the Trinity, through Christ's birth, his cross and his rising, through angels and saints, and through creation itself: the sun's light, the fire's glow, the wind, the sea, the earth, the rock. Third, the circle. Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me. Christ beneath me, above me, on my right, on my left. The prayer turns slowly, like someone checking every side of the road before stepping out. Fourth, the people. Christ in the heart of everyone who thinks of me, in the mouth of everyone who speaks of me, in every eye that sees me, in every ear that hears me. And this whole week fits inside it. Ignatius, Polycarp, Perpetua, Antony: each one walked out a door into something hard, and none of them went alone.
screen: `LORICA: ARMOR IN WORDS.` · `RISING THROUGH SUN AND ROCK.` · `CHRIST ON EVERY SIDE.` · `IN EVERY EYE THAT SEES ME.` · then, large: `CHRIST WITH ME.`

segments.voice: Stand facing a door, the one you'll walk through next. Turn your attention slowly around you, one breath each: before, behind, right, left, above, below. If you pray, say Christ with me at each; if not, simply notice every side, and the faces waiting out there.
The Breastplate. A prayer worn like armor, with Christ on every side, above and below, and in every face on the road.
Your line: christ with me. On every side of the road, and in every face on it. That's the week.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Saint Patrick's Breastplate, often in a hymn version, especially around his feast day; many people keep a prayer card of it near the door.

pairs: a story people tell about the road

myth: the Breastplate is a charm to keep the body safe from harm
it surrounds the singer with Christ, and finds him in every face met on the road.
the deer on the road is told as a story people tell
tradition, not a signature, ties the prayer to Patrick.
the prayer stops at the singer's own body
it goes on: Christ in every eye that sees me, every ear that hears me.

fork.setup: your aunt starts work as a nurse and dreads her hardest patients. which line of the Breastplate fits her first shift?
options: Christ in every eye that sees me, the hard patients too.
the deer: she can slip past difficult people unseen.
the rock: be hard, so nothing gets through to her.
fork.reveal: the Breastplate doesn't stop at the singer. it ends with Christ in the heart, mouth, eye and ear of everyone met on the road.

original.note: Latin for body armor, a breastplate: the name for this kind of protective prayer.

chat.says: abuela pinned a prayer card by my door before my shift: christ before me, behind me. lucky charm?
options: Not a charm. It's armor of words: Christ on every side, and in every face at work.
Kind of. Patrick sang it so enemies couldn't see him, like a shield that hides you.
